definitions.definition: A mapping between two systems that shows they have the same structure or pattern, even if they look different on the surface.
definitions.example: A map of a subway system is isomorphic to the actual subway lines because the connections between stations are the same, even though the map is not the real thing.

definitions.definition: A branch of engineering that studies how to make systems behave in a desired way by using feedback to correct errors.
definitions.example: A thermostat uses control theory to keep your room at the temperature you set by turning the heater on and off.

definitions.definition: A type of controller that uses three methods to correct errors: Proportional (based on current error), Integral (based on past errors), and Derivative (based on how fast the error is changing).
definitions.example: A self-driving car uses a PID controller to stay in its lane: it corrects based on how far off it is now (P), how long it has been off (I), and how quickly it is drifting (D).

definitions.definition: A mathematical formula that describes how a system responds to inputs, like a recipe that tells you what output you get for a given input.
definitions.example: If you press the gas pedal in a car (input), the transfer function describes how fast the car will go (output).

definitions.definition: The desired target value that a control system tries to reach and maintain.
definitions.example: The temperature you set on your thermostat, like 72°F, is the setpoint.

definitions.definition: The ability of a control system to ignore or reduce the effect of unwanted outside influences.
definitions.example: A noise-canceling headphone rejects the disturbance of background noise so you can hear your music clearly.

definitions.definition: Whether a system can be moved from any starting state to any desired state using the right inputs.
definitions.example: A car is controllable because you can steer it to any parking spot in a lot, as long as you have enough space.

definitions.definition: Whether you can figure out what is happening inside a system just by looking at its outputs.
definitions.example: You can tell if a person is sick (internal state) by their symptoms (outputs) like a fever or cough.

definitions.definition: The idea that God guides and takes care of everything in the universe, like a parent watching over a child.
definitions.example: Believing that things happen for a reason and that God has a plan is trusting in providence.

definitions.definition: The concept that God has ultimate authority and control over everything.
definitions.example: A king has sovereignty over his kingdom, meaning he makes the final decisions.

definitions.definition: The belief that God has already decided the final outcome or destiny of every person before they are born.
definitions.example: Some people believe that God has predestined who will go to heaven.

definitions.definition: The ability of a person to make their own choices without being forced by outside forces.
definitions.example: Choosing what to eat for breakfast is an exercise of free will.

definitions.definition: The process of becoming more holy or morally good over time, often with God's help.
definitions.example: A person trying to be more patient and kind is going through sanctification.

definitions.definition: The ultimate purpose or goal of something.
definitions.example: The telos of a seed is to become a fully grown tree.

definitions.definition: A mathematical way of analyzing systems that change over time, using a special transformation to make calculations easier.
definitions.example: It is like translating a sentence into a code that is easier to solve, then translating the answer back.

definitions.definition: In control theory, the system or process that is being controlled.
definitions.example: In a cruise control system, the car is the plant that the controller tries to keep at a constant speed.

definitions.definition: A factor that determines how strongly a controller responds to the current error.
definitions.example: If you are driving and you are slightly off-center, proportional gain is how much you turn the wheel to correct it right now.

definitions.definition: A factor that determines how strongly a controller responds to errors that have built up over time.
definitions.example: If you have been drifting off course for a while, integral gain increases the correction to finally get back on track.

definitions.definition: A factor that determines how strongly a controller responds to how fast the error is changing.
definitions.example: If you are drifting off course quickly, derivative gain makes a bigger correction to prevent overshooting.

definitions.definition: A rule that tells whether a feedback system will stay stable or start oscillating out of control.
definitions.example: It is like checking if a microphone and speaker setup will cause a screeching feedback loop.

definitions.definition: A mathematical description of a system without feedback, so it does not correct itself based on the output.
definitions.example: A toaster that just heats for a set time, regardless of whether the toast is done, is an open-loop system.

definitions.definition: Mathematical points in a system's description that indicate it is unstable and will grow uncontrollably.
definitions.example: Like a snowball rolling downhill that gets bigger and faster on its own.

definitions.definition: The difference between the desired value and the actual value after the system has settled down.
definitions.example: If your thermostat keeps the room at 70°F but you set it to 72°F, the steady-state error is 2°F.

definitions.definition: God's help that comes before a person makes a choice, preparing them to do good.
definitions.example: It is like a coach giving you advice before you even start the race.

definitions.definition: A force that reduces oscillations or vibrations in a system, making it settle down smoothly.
definitions.example: Shock absorbers on a car provide damping so the car does not keep bouncing after hitting a bump.

definitions.definition: When a system goes past its target before settling down.
definitions.example: If you turn the shower knob too far and the water gets too hot before you adjust it, that is overshoot.

definitions.definition: A process where the output of a system is used to reduce the difference between the actual and desired state, keeping things stable.
definitions.example: A thermostat turns off the heater when the room reaches the set temperature, preventing it from getting too hot.

definitions.definition: A process where the output of a system amplifies the difference, causing it to grow and become unstable.
definitions.example: A microphone held too close to a speaker creates a loud screech because the sound keeps getting amplified.

definitions.definition: The study of how parts of a system are connected or arranged, especially in terms of loops and pathways.
definitions.example: The layout of a city's subway map shows the topology of the train lines.

definitions.definition: To reduce the strength or effect of something.
definitions.example: Sunglasses attenuate the brightness of the sun so you can see better.

definitions.definition: A measure of how much a signal is amplified as it goes around a feedback loop.
definitions.example: If you speak into a microphone and the sound comes out louder, the loop gain is greater than 1.

definitions.definition: The belief that God created the universe but does not actively interfere with it, like a clockmaker who winds a clock and lets it run.
definitions.example: A deist believes God set the world in motion but does not answer prayers or perform miracles.

definitions.definition: The belief that God is actively involved in the world and interacts with people.
definitions.example: A theist believes God answers prayers and guides events.

definitions.definition: A statement or situation that seems to contradict itself but might still be true.
definitions.example: The saying 'less is more' is a paradox because it seems to say the opposite of what is expected.

definitions.definition: A sin that, according to some Christian beliefs, cannot be forgiven because it represents a complete and final rejection of God.
definitions.example: In the Bible, Jesus talks about blasphemy against the Holy Spirit as an unforgivable sin.

definitions.definition: The act of abandoning or renouncing one's religious faith.
definitions.example: If someone who was a Christian decides they no longer believe in God, that is apostasy.

definitions.definition: A measure of how much delay or phase shift a feedback system can handle before it becomes unstable.
definitions.example: It is like how much extra slack a rope has before it breaks.

definitions.definition: A measure of how much the amplification in a feedback system can increase before it becomes unstable.
definitions.example: It is like how much louder you can turn up a microphone before it starts screeching.

definitions.definition: A follower of John Calvin's teachings, which emphasize God's complete control over salvation and that some people are predestined to be saved.
definitions.example: Calvinists believe that once a person is truly saved, they cannot lose their salvation.

definitions.definition: A follower of Jacobus Arminius's teachings, which emphasize human free will and the possibility of losing salvation.
definitions.example: Arminians believe that a person can choose to turn away from God after being saved.

definitions.definition: The belief that once a person is truly saved, they can never lose their salvation.
definitions.example: The phrase 'once saved, always saved' describes eternal security.

definitions.definition: To express something in a precise, structured, often mathematical way.
definitions.example: A recipe formalizes the steps to bake a cake so anyone can follow them exactly.

definitions.definition: Based on observation or experience, not just theory.
definitions.example: A doctor uses empirical evidence from tests to diagnose a disease.

definitions.definition: The ability of a theory to be proven wrong by evidence or experiment.
definitions.example: The statement 'all swans are white' is falsifiable because finding one black swan proves it false.

definitions.definition: The study of how systems control themselves and communicate, especially through feedback loops.
definitions.example: Cybernetics looks at how a thermostat, a robot, or even a living organism regulates itself.

definitions.definition: The study of how things appear to our consciousness or experience, rather than what they are in reality.
definitions.example: Phenomenology of a sunset is about the feeling of awe and beauty, not the physics of light.

definitions.definition: Relating to the end of the world or the final destiny of humanity.
definitions.example: Discussions about heaven, hell, and the apocalypse are eschatological.

definitions.definition: A state or set of states that a system tends to move toward over time.
definitions.example: A marble in a bowl will always roll to the bottom, which is the attractor.

definitions.definition: A basic statement or rule that is accepted as true without proof, used as a starting point for further reasoning.
definitions.example: In geometry, 'a straight line is the shortest distance between two points' is an axiom.
